lesson.title: Mind the Minus: Subtracting Polynomials Correctly
lesson.summary: Subtracting polynomials means distributing a negative sign across every single term of the second polynomial before combining like terms, the one step that causes nearly every error in this skill.
lesson.body:
Subtracting one polynomial from another looks similar to adding them, but it hides an important difference. When you compute (A) - (B) for two polynomials A and B, you cannot simply drop both sets of parentheses the way you can with addition. Subtracting a polynomial means adding the opposite of every one of its terms, so the minus sign in front of the second polynomial must be distributed across each term inside it before anything else happens.

The safest way to handle this is to treat subtraction as multiplying the second polynomial by -1 and distributing that -1 across every term, flipping each term's sign individually. Once every sign inside the second polynomial has been flipped, the rest of the process is identical to adding polynomials: combine terms with matching variable parts, typically finishing in standard form.

Let's subtract (x^2 + 7x - 9) from (3x^2 - 5x + 4), which means computing (3x^2 - 5x + 4) - (x^2 + 7x - 9). Distribute the negative sign across the second polynomial: x^2 becomes -x^2, 7x becomes -7x, and -9 becomes +9. The expression is now 3x^2 - 5x + 4 - x^2 - 7x + 9. Combine the x^2 terms: 3x^2 - x^2 = 2x^2. Combine the x terms: -5x - 7x = -12x. Combine the constants: 4 + 9 = 13. The result is 2x^2 - 12x + 13. To check, substitute x = 2. The first polynomial gives 3(4) - 10 + 4 = 6, and the second gives 4 + 14 - 9 = 9, so the difference should be 6 - 9 = -3. The simplified result at x = 2 gives 2(4) - 24 + 13 = 8 - 24 + 13 = -3. Both match, confirming the subtraction was done correctly.

The single most common mistake here is flipping the sign on only the first term of the second polynomial and forgetting the rest, treating (x^2 + 7x - 9) as if subtracting it only changes x^2 into -x^2 while leaving 7x and -9 untouched. Every term inside those parentheses must have its sign flipped, not just the one closest to the minus sign.

Just as with addition, subtraction can involve terms that do not have a match in the other polynomial; those terms simply carry through, keeping whatever sign resulted from distributing the negative. It is also worth noting that when two polynomials of the same degree are subtracted, their leading terms can cancel completely, leaving a result with a smaller degree than either original polynomial, similar to what can happen when adding polynomials. This is one more reason to always distribute the negative sign fully before combining anything, rather than trying to combine terms while a subtraction is still pending.

With adding and subtracting polynomials both in place, alongside combining like terms, degree, leading coefficient, and standard form, you now have a complete toolkit for working with polynomial expressions confidently. These same combining skills carry forward directly into multiplying polynomials and eventually solving polynomial equations, so the care taken here in tracking signs and matching terms pays off throughout the rest of algebra.
